title: Lesson 3: Hospitality as Mission
description: Using your home, your table, and your welcome as frontline tools for the gospel.

blocks.text: In Lesson 2 you began with prayer and wrote three to five names on your prayer card. The next two rhythms belong together: Listen and Eat. Listening helps someone feel known, and an open table gives listening room to happen. Together they make up much of what the Bible calls hospitality.

blocks.title: Stay with Us
blocks.text:
On the Sunday Jesus rose, two of His followers walked from Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were heartbroken. Their hopes had died on a cross. As they talked, "Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:15-16).

Jesus knew everything that had happened. He had lived it. Yet He started with a question: "What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?" They stood still, looking sad, and Jesus asked again, "What things?" (Luke 24:17-19). Then He let them pour out the whole story of their grief and confusion.

Only after listening did Jesus open the Scriptures to them. When they reached the village, they urged their traveling companion, "Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent" (Luke 24:29). So the stranger sat down at their table. "He took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him" (Luke 24:30-31).

Look at what happened on that road. The risen Lord asked questions and listened to a sad story He already knew. Then a simple meal became the place where two friends recognized Him. Afterward they said, "Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?" (Luke 24:32). Listening opened their hearts, and the table opened their eyes.
3.1 - Think of a time someone really listened to you. What did they do that made you feel heard?
Listen: Help Someone Feel Known

Many people go through whole weeks without anyone asking them a real question and waiting for the answer. When you slow down and listen to someone's story, their hopes, their fears, and what they are carrying, you give them a rare gift. Without saying a word, you tell them they matter. People do not care how much you know until they know how much you care.
Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.

Jesus, who had every answer, asked questions anyway. When a blind man named Bartimaeus cried out to Him, Jesus asked, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51). Good listening has that posture: you listen to the person in front of you while quietly asking the Holy Spirit what is really going on and how to love them well.

blocks.title: Ask, Ask Again, Remember
content: Ask. Use open questions that cannot be answered with yes or no. What has your week been like? How did you end up living here? What are you looking forward to?

Ask again. The first answer is usually the surface. Follow it with a second question: What was that like? Tell me more. "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (Proverbs 20:5).
Remember. Write down what you heard, pray about it with your prayer card, and ask about it the next time you see them. Remembering is what turns a conversation into a friendship.

blocks.text: 3.2 - Choose one name from your prayer card. What is one open question you could ask them this week, and what second question could you follow it with?
Eat: The Table Jesus Set

Jesus ate His way through the Gospels. He ate with tax collectors and religious leaders, with fishermen and friends, and even with the man who would betray Him. He was at the table with the wrong people so often that His critics called Him "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Luke 7:34). It described His mission.
Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them."

The New Testament word for hospitality, philoxenia, means love of strangers. It reaches past friends, easy people, and people who will invite you back. "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers" (Hebrews 13:2). Paul tells believers to "seek to show hospitality" (Romans 12:13). Seeking means you go looking for chances to welcome people instead of waiting until the house is clean.

Hospitality is not the same as entertaining. Entertaining puts the spotlight on your home, your cooking, and you. Hospitality puts it on your guest, so they feel seen, safe, and wanted. The size of your home has nothing to do with the size of your welcome.

blocks.title: The Open Table
content: Hospitality is a seat at your table, your full attention, an unhurried conversation, room for people who are not like you, and a simple meal, even takeout on paper plates, shared gladly.
Hospitality is not a perfect house, a fancy menu, a performance, a sales pitch, or a dinner saved for the friends who will invite you back.

blocks.text: 3.3 - Where has the pressure to impress kept you from opening your home or table more freely?
Pull Up a Chair

Hospitality does not have to start with a dinner party. Invite a coworker to lunch. Ask a neighbor over for coffee. Add one more seat to a meal you were already going to have. And let others host you too. When Jesus sent His disciples out, He told them to stay in the homes that welcomed them, "eating and drinking what they provide" (Luke 10:7). Sometimes the best way to open your table is to sit gladly at someone else's.

Then bring the Listen rhythm to the table. Put your phone away. Ask, ask again, and remember. A meal gives a conversation time to go deeper than a wave across the yard ever could. Opening your table takes some courage, because people may say no or the talk may feel awkward at first. But you do not go alone. The Jesus who drew near on the Emmaus road has promised to be with you always (Matthew 28:20).
3.4 - Write one specific plan to open your table in the next 30 days. Name the person, the occasion, and the date you will aim for.
Why You Welcome Strangers

Here is the deepest reason for hospitality: God welcomed you first. Paul reminds believers that they were once "strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world", until Christ brought them near by His blood (Ephesians 2:12-13). You were the outsider, and Jesus pulled out a chair for you. Welcomed people learn to welcome others.
Show hospitality to one another without grumbling. As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace.

Every open table is a small picture of a bigger one. Scripture describes the end of the story as a feast: "Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9). When you listen well and set an extra place, you give your neighbors a taste of the welcome Jesus offers them. If your door has mostly stayed closed, you do not need guilt, only a beginning. One good question and one empty chair are enough to start.
Lesson 3 Review

On the road to Emmaus, Jesus listened to two grieving friends, and they recognized Him at the table. Listening helps people feel known, and the table gives listening room to grow into friendship. Ask, ask again, and remember. Open your table to strangers, not to impress them but to welcome them, because in Christ, God welcomed you first.
In the next lesson, you will learn the fourth rhythm, Serve, and see how Jesus showed the way when He knelt to wash His disciples' feet.

The BLESS rhythms are adapted from BLESS: 5 Everyday Ways to Love Your Neighbor and Change the World by Dave Ferguson and Jon Ferguson. This lesson also draws on writing about hospitality by David Mathis and Matt Chandler.
